results.summary:
How a Lighthouse Lens Works

• A lighthouse lamp is weak and spreads its glow in every direction, fading before it reaches a ship over the horizon.
• The trick that made lighthouses useful for ships far out at sea was not a stronger flame, but a better way of aiming the light that already existed.
• Augustin Fresnel built a lens in 1822 that did exactly this, using many thin glass rings and prisms arranged in a circle.
• Each ring bends the light from the lamp at the centre, leaving in a flat, narrow beam instead of spreading out.
• The result is a lens that is far lighter than a solid one and captures much more of the lamp's light.
• Large lenses turn slowly on a bed of liquid mercury or on ball bearings, driven by a clockwork motor.
• The time between flashes is a signature, indicating the location of a lighthouse.
• Some lights use red or green panels to mark dangerous sectors, while others use white or coloured lights to indicate safe courses.

results.summary:
Lighthouses: A Short History of Light on the Coast

- Page title provides a brief overview of the content within.
- The page discusses the history of lighthouses, starting with their use for navigation and safety in ancient civilizations.
- Key facts about lighthouses include:
  - The first lighthouse was built on the island of Pharos in ancient Egypt.
  - The design of the Pharos lighthouse was later adopted by other civilizations.
  - The French engineer Augustin Fresnel improved the design of the Pharos lighthouse with his invention of the Fresnel lens.
- The history of lighthouses continues with their use as beacons for navigation, guiding ships and other vessels.
- The use of radio beacons and radar systems has replaced the need for lighthouses, and automation of their lighting has become the norm.
- The page concludes with the current state of lighthouses, with many being saved and preserved, and some becoming museums or tourist attractions.
